learningObjective: Understand why IREE separates compiler and runtime and its edge-deployment implication.

canonicalClaims.claim: IREE separates a heavyweight AOT compiler from a small embeddable runtime library so that edge/mobile devices can execute compiled `.vmfb` bytecode without hosting the MLIR toolchain.
nonImplications: Does not imply the compiler cannot be embedded for JIT flows.
Does not imply the runtime is limited to edge use.

misconceptions.claim: IREE bytecode requires the compiler at runtime.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Compiled artifacts run without the compiler.

misconceptions.claim: The IREE runtime is only for development.
misconceptions.whyWrong: It is a production runtime library.

misconceptions.claim: Compiler and runtime are the same binary.
misconceptions.whyWrong: They are structurally separate for size and deployment reasons.

misconceptions.claim: IREE separation implies compiled artifacts are portable across all backends without recompilation.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Artifacts contain target-specific code; different targets typically need separate compiles.

implementationFacts: Runtime library: `libireert.*`, embeddable in C/C++/Python hosts.
Bytecode container: `.vmfb`, contains module + device artifacts.
